text: Bristell NG5 LSA vs. Cessna 172 — Which Is Right for Your Training? | Diego Suarez
Bristell NG5 LSA vs. Cessna 172: Which Aircraft Is Right for Your Training?
At Bowman Field, most training happens in one of two airplanes: a modern Light-Sport Aircraft like the
. They're both capable trainers, but they're very different machines, and the right choice depends on what you want to do with your certificate.
This is a student-pilot comparison from someone who has flown both at KLOU. No brand loyalty, no affiliate links. Just what each airplane is good at, what each costs, and how to pick between them.
The two aircraft at a glance
Verify the specific aircraft’s current certification documents
Configuration varies; verify the specific aircraft
Do not use the former Sport Pilot weight limit; MOSAIC changed the framework
Verify engine and equipment from the aircraft records
Verify published performance for the exact configuration
Verify the engine and POH/AFM fuel approval before planning fuel
Panel and installed equipment vary by aircraft
Mix of steam and glass by airframe
Private Pilot training; Sport Pilot eligibility depends on current rules and the exact aircraft
Confirm current wet rate with the operator
Confirm current wet rate with the operator

Both aircraft can take a student from zero time to a Private Pilot certificate. The choice between them is less about capability and more about cost structure, certificate target, and what you want in the cockpit.

The former Light-Sport Aircraft definition used familiar weight, seat, and speed limits. That is no longer the right test for a Sport Pilot operation. The FAA’s MOSAIC rules, effective October 22, 2025 for Sport Pilot privileges, moved the operational aircraft criteria to 14 CFR §61.316 and allow a broader range of aircraft when the applicable requirements and endorsements are met. Start with the FAA’s
and verify the exact aircraft before training.

A Bristell NG5 may be operated under different certification and equipment configurations. Use the specific aircraft’s airworthiness certificate, operating limitations, and operating handbook—not a generic model description—to determine what training and operations are appropriate.

The Cessna 172 is a standard-category trainer with model-specific equipment and performance. Whether a particular aircraft can be used for a given training or Sport Pilot operation requires verification under the current rule and the operator’s procedures.

The Bristell is light on the controls. Small inputs produce immediate, visible results. That's excellent for a beginner because it teaches responsive flying from the first hour — no slop in the feedback loop. The tradeoff: it's less forgiving of over-control. Students tend to pilot-induced-oscillate on their first few landings until they learn to trust smaller inputs.

The Cessna 172 is heavier in the controls, particularly in roll. You have to mean your inputs. That teaches a different flavor of discipline — you're commanding the airplane, not suggesting to it. Students who started on 172s sometimes feel over-controlled when they move to lighter aircraft; students who started on lighter aircraft sometimes feel hamfisted moving up.
Neither is better for learning. Both produce good pilots.

Both airplanes have benign stall behavior — a clear buffet, a recoverable break, no tendency to spin with normal weight-and-balance. The Bristell's stall feels crisper and happens at a lower airspeed. The 172's stall feels more ponderous and starts at a higher airspeed, with more pronounced nose-drop.

The 172 wins this one convincingly. More mass, more rudder authority, higher published crosswind component. The Bristell is lighter and gets pushed around more by gusts — not dangerous, but students notice it and develop crosswind technique faster because the airplane makes you.

text: Your First Discovery Flight at Bowman Field — What to Expect | Diego Suarez
Your First Discovery Flight at Bowman Field
If you've been thinking about flying lessons but haven't pulled the trigger, the thing stopping you is probably not money or time. It's that you don't actually know what flying a small airplane
like. You can watch YouTube forever and still not know whether you'll love it, hate it, get motion sick, or find out it's the thing you've been looking for your whole life.

A discovery flight is how you find out. About an hour in a real airplane at Bowman Field (KLOU), with an instructor in the right seat and you in the left. Hands on the controls from the time the wheels leave the ground. No commitment, no brochure, just a flight.
This article is what I tell first-timers before their discovery flight, so they walk in knowing what's going to happen and walk out with a clear answer to "is this for me."
What a discovery flight is — and isn't

an introductory lesson. Around an hour of airplane time, preceded by a short ground briefing and followed by a debrief. You sit in the left seat. The instructor explains what's happening, demonstrates, then hands over the controls. The flight logs legally in your logbook if you decide to keep going.

a scenic tour (though the view is great). It's not a simulator session. It's not a sales pitch — good instructors will answer your questions honestly, including "is flying a smart use of my time and money?" If it feels like a sales pitch, that's information about the instructor, not about flying.
One more distinction: a discovery flight is not a test. You don't need to perform. Most first-timers fly better than they expect because the airplane is more stable than they expect.

Discovery flights at Bowman Field should be scheduled in an approved training aircraft with an appropriately authorized instructor. The exact airplane can vary by provider, maintenance, weather, insurance, and operator policy, so confirm the aircraft and instructor before booking.
You should be able to see enough outside to connect the airplane's attitude with what the instruments show.
A good first lesson keeps the handling simple enough that you can feel pitch, bank, trim, and rudder without overload.
Whether the panel is glass or round dials, the first goal is basic orientation, not memorizing every display.
Calm morning or evening air usually gives a cleaner first impression than a bumpy midday flight.
The right aircraft is the one that fits the lesson, is approved for the operation, and is actually available on the schedule.
Minute-by-minute: what your discovery flight looks like

Park at Bowman Field and come in to the office. I'll meet you, we'll do a short intake — basic info, a signature on a liability release, and a quick conversation about what you'd like out of the flight. "I want to see if I like it" is a great answer. "I want to see if I can handle the controls" is also great. No wrong answers.
If you showed up anxious, we'll talk about that too. A lot of first-timers do. Anxiety in this context is information, not a problem.

Before we go to the airplane, I'll walk through what's going to happen. The basics of how the airplane flies (lift, drag, thrust, weight — the minimum you need to follow along). What each control does. How I'll hand off and take back controls. What to expect during takeoff and landing. What you'll feel in a turn. How to handle your hands and feet so you're working with the airplane, not against it.
This briefing is short on purpose. The airplane teaches faster than a whiteboard.

We walk around the airplane together. I show you what I'm checking and why — fuel quantity, oil, control surfaces, tires, general airworthiness. You don't have to memorize anything. The point is to see that we don't just jump in and go; flying is procedural for good reason.

You sit in the left seat. I'm in the right. I handle the startup and get us to the runway — you feel the airplane come alive and start moving. Your feet may rest lightly on the rudder pedals so you can feel the steering. Your hands are free.

I do the takeoff. There's too much happening in the first thirty seconds for a first-timer to manage the controls cleanly, and there's no learning benefit in trying. But you'll feel the acceleration, watch the ground peel away, and notice how quickly we're flying. Bowman Field sits at the edge of residential Louisville, and the departure view is genuinely beautiful.
This is the part the flight is built around. Once we're clear of Bowman's traffic pattern, I'll hand the controls over to you.
You'll start with straight-and-level flight — just holding altitude and heading. That's harder than it sounds and also easier than it sounds. You'll get the feel for it in a few minutes.

Then climbs and descents. Then turns. We'll fly over Louisville — Churchill Downs is typically visible from our normal practice area, along with the Ohio River, downtown, and whichever bridge you drive across to get to work.
If you want to try a little steeper turn, we'll do that. If you want to hold altitude and just enjoy cruising, we'll do that. It's your hour.
The common reaction at this point: "wait, it's actually doing what I'm telling it to do." Yes. Airplanes fly. That's what they do.

We return to Bowman. I take the controls back for the approach and landing. You'll watch how a real landing happens — the speed management, the descent path, the flare, the touchdown. Most first-timers tell me the landing was their favorite part of the flight, which makes sense: it's where all the energy of the airplane resolves into stillness.

Back in the office, we talk about what you felt. What worked, what didn't, what surprised you. I log the flight in your new logbook if you want one — those hours count toward any future certificate you pursue.

If you want to schedule a follow-up lesson, we can. If you want to go home and think about it, perfect. If you've decided flying isn't for you, you saved yourself thousands of dollars by finding out today.
Will you actually fly the plane?

Yes. "Hands-on controls" is not a marketing phrase. You'll do straight-and-level, climbs, descents, turns — the same fundamental maneuvers every pilot learns on their first lesson. I'll keep hands close to my own controls the whole time (standard procedure), but the flying is yours.
What to bring / what to wear
— the sky is bright and most training aircraft have a lot of glare through the windows. Non-polarized is slightly better for reading glass-panel displays, but any sunglasses beat squinting.
— you'll use rudder pedals. No flip-flops.
— Bowman Field ramp temperature is usually a few degrees warmer than surrounding Louisville, but cockpit comfort varies.
— not a heavy one. You want blood sugar steady and stomach calm. Coffee is fine; avoid anything you might regret at 1,000 feet AGL.
That's really the whole list. You don't need a headset (I provide one), a logbook (I provide one if you want to start), or any prior knowledge. You just need to show up.
A lot of first-timers worry about this and it's almost never a problem on calm-morning discovery flights. If you're prone to car sickness, let me know beforehand — we'll pick a smoother time of day.
You won't be graded. Everyone's first flight has clumsy moments. The airplane forgives far more than a car does.
I handle all radio work. If you want to know what's being said, I'll translate; if you want to ignore it and focus on flying, that's fine too.
You're not navigating. We don't leave visual range of Bowman Field.

If you want to continue toward a certificate, we can plan next steps — medical certificate, ground knowledge, a realistic training schedule. If you want to stop after one flight, you got a great hour and an honest answer to a question most people never ask. Both outcomes are legitimate.
Your discovery flight hour also logs toward whatever certificate you eventually pursue — Sport Pilot, Private Pilot, or otherwise. Nothing is wasted.
How much does a discovery flight at Bowman Field cost?
The current price is published on the
— reach out and I'll confirm it before you commit to anything.
How long is the actual flight?
About an hour in the airplane, plus 30–40 minutes of briefing and debrief on the ground. Budget about 2 hours total at the airport.
Can I bring someone to watch?
Yes. They can sit at the airport or watch from the ramp (weather permitting). They cannot ride in the airplane during a discovery flight — there are only two seats, and you need one of them.
What if the weather is bad?
We reschedule. I don't squeeze discovery flights into marginal weather. The point is for you to have a clean, honest experience — not to survive turbulence.
Can I take photos during the flight?
Yes. A phone is fine. GoPro is fine. Keep it stashed during takeoff and landing.
Do I need to know anything before I come?
No. Read nothing, watch nothing, learn nothing. Show up. The airplane is the teacher.
A little planning makes the first flight easier.

The radio. I handle all radio work. If you want to know what's being said, I'll translate; if you want to ignore it and focus on flying, that's fine too.
Getting lost. You're not navigating. We don't leave visual range of Bowman Field.

If you want to continue toward a certificate, we can plan next steps — medical certificate, ground knowledge, a realistic training schedule. If you want to stop after one flight, you got a great hour and an honest answer to a question most people never ask. Both outcomes are legitimate.
Your discovery flight hour also logs toward whatever certificate you eventually pursue — Sport Pilot, Private Pilot, or otherwise. Nothing is wasted.

text: AC 61-65K Endorsement Lookup | FAA Endorsements List
Every FAA Endorsement a Student Pilot Should Understand

An FAA endorsement is a logbook entry or written statement from an authorized instructor. It documents that a pilot received required training, is prepared for a test, or is authorized for a specific operation. For student pilots, endorsements are what turn training milestones into legal privileges: first solo, solo cross-country, knowledge-test eligibility, checkride readiness, and later currency events.
The FAA's model endorsement language lives in Advisory Circular 61-65K. That circular is the source layer.
is the search layer: a free AC 61-65K endorsement lookup tool that lets you search by endorsement ID, FAR citation, alias, task, or checkride workflow.

An endorsement is not a casual note. It is the instructor's certification that a specific regulatory requirement has been met. Some endorsements authorize an action, such as a student solo. Others document readiness, such as a knowledge test or practical test recommendation. Some are tied to time windows, aircraft make and model, route approval, airspace, or a particular training event.

That is why copying random endorsement wording is risky. The correct question is not only "what text do I need?" It is "which rule applies, what training or review happened, who can sign this, and what limitation or expiration applies?"

Before first solo, a student pilot normally needs both pre-solo knowledge and pre-solo flight training documented. In the AC 61-65K Appendix A structure, those are commonly searched as A.3 and A.4. The knowledge endorsement connects to the pre-solo knowledge test. The flight-training endorsement connects to proficiency in the specific make and model.

That distinction matters. A student can be smart on the ground but not yet proficient in the airplane. A student can fly well but still need the written pre-solo knowledge check. Both pieces support the solo decision.

The first solo authorization is the endorsement many students remember most. It is normally tied to a specific make and model and expires after the allowed solo period. The common student-solo cluster includes first 90-calendar-day solo authority and additional 90-calendar-day renewals.
for the full pre-solo, first-solo, renewal, nearby-airport, Class B, and TSA context.

Solo cross-country has its own endorsement logic. A student may need an initial solo cross-country endorsement, a route-specific endorsement for a particular flight, or an endorsement for repeated solo cross-country flights within a defined route and distance. These are not interchangeable.
For the detailed A.9, A.10, and A.11 flow, use the

Most FAA knowledge tests require some form of authorization before the applicant can sit for the exam. For private pilot students, this often means a ground instructor, flight instructor, or approved home-study course certifies that the applicant is prepared. The endorsement is not just a scheduling formality; it is the bridge between study and official testing.
If you are preparing for the written, pair this article with the
and use Simply Endorsed CFI when you need the AC 61-65K model text.
FAA Private Pilot Written Test Study Guide

Before a practical test, the applicant's logbook and application package need to show the right training, readiness, and knowledge-test-deficiency review. A common pattern is practical-test preparation within the required timing window, review of missed knowledge-test areas when required, and the certificate-specific practical-test recommendation.
Private pilot applicants can start with the
. Commercial, instrument, and CFI applicants have their own endorsement clusters.

If an applicant fails a knowledge or practical test, the next attempt may require added training and a retest endorsement. The point is not paperwork theater. The instructor is certifying that the deficient areas were addressed and that the applicant is prepared to retest.
After the checkride: flight reviews and IPCs

Endorsements do not stop after the certificate. Pilots continue to see signoffs for flight reviews, WINGS completion, instrument proficiency checks, aircraft transitions, and other privileges. A flight review endorsement is different from an IPC endorsement, and both are different from a practical-test recommendation.
For recurrent training, start with the

Aircraft-specific endorsements include common transition items such as complex, high-performance, high-altitude, and tailwheel. These are easy to confuse because pilots often talk about them as a group, but each has its own rule basis and training purpose.
If you are looking for the tailwheel path, use the
. For the broader group, use the
How to use Simply Endorsed CFI
When you need the exact model text, open

and search the phrase you actually have in your head: "first solo," "61.87," "A.6," "BFR," "tailwheel," "IPC," or "CFI checkride." The tool returns matching endorsements with ID, FAR context, aliases, explanation, and related paths.
Use the tool as a fast reference, then verify the pilot's actual certificate path, training record, timing, aircraft, and current FAA guidance before signing anything.
Using a first-solo endorsement when the flight actually needs a solo cross-country or nearby-airport endorsement.
Forgetting that some student solo endorsements expire after a defined period.
Treating A.1 and A.2 as optional paperwork instead of checkride-readiness and deficiency-review context.
Confusing a flight review, WINGS completion, IPC, and practical-test recommendation.
Copying model text without confirming that the instructor is authorized and the applicant actually meets the requirement.

Endorsements are the paper trail behind pilot privileges. They show what was trained, reviewed, authorized, or recommended. Learn the purpose first, then look up the exact wording. That is the job Simply Endorsed CFI was built for.

text: How to Study for the FAA Private Pilot Written Test | Diego Suarez
How to Study for the FAA Private Pilot Written Test

The Private Pilot knowledge test — also called the written, even though you take it on a computer — is the part of flight training most students put off the longest and then regret putting off. It's not hard. It's tedious. The material spans enough ground that with zero plan you can drift for months, and without the written passed, your progress in the airplane starts to stall as checkride season approaches.

This is the study plan I give my students. I'm an FAA Certificated Flight Instructor and Advanced Ground Instructor based in Louisville — the ground-school endorsement for this test is literally my job. The plan below will get you through the written cleanly, on the first try, and without wasting time on drills that don't matter.
Plenty of time; most students finish in 60–90 minutes.
You need at least 42 out of 60 correct.
There's one in the Louisville area.
Confirm current fee when you schedule.
You'll walk out knowing your score.
The test draws from the FAA's published question bank. The exact wording of questions can vary slightly release to release, but the subject distribution is stable.
Where to take it in Louisville

PSI CATS testing centers administer FAA knowledge tests on behalf of the FAA. There is a PSI CATS location in the Louisville area. Confirm the current location and hours when you schedule, as testing center details can change. You schedule directly through PSI's website (psiexams.com), not through the testing center itself.

The center-day experience: arrive early, ID check, secure your belongings, take the test at a computer terminal. You'll be monitored. No phone, no notes, no personal calculator — the system provides a digital E6B and plotter. Scratch-paper work is allowed; you turn everything in at the end.
The knowledge-test endorsement (and why it matters)
You can't take the knowledge test without an endorsement. Any of the following works:
— some FAA-approved self-study programs include this automatically on completion.

That last option matters for cost-conscious students. If you self-study with an approved course, your software may issue the endorsement automatically. If you study on your own or with a local instructor, you'll need your ground instructor or CFI to sign you off.
For the exact AC 61-65K knowledge-test wording, use
as a quick FAA endorsement lookup before you schedule the exam. For the bigger picture around solo, checkride, recurrent, and aircraft signoffs, read the

If you'd like to work through the weak subject areas with someone who can explain them — that's the core of what I do as an FAA Certificated Flight Instructor and Advanced Ground Instructor. Reach out and we can plan around your schedule.
You have three core elements, in this order of importance:
These are the FAA-published handbooks. They are the real authority on everything on the test:
— use the current edition listed by the FAA.
; it supersedes the older AC 00-6 / 00-45 references.
All of these are free PDFs on the FAA's website. Print versions run $30–$60 each. For a first read, PDF on a big screen is fine.

This is where the efficiency gains live. Test prep software feeds you questions from the actual FAA bank, tracks your performance, and focuses you on weak areas. Without it, you can study the right material for 200 hours and still miss questions whose phrasing trips you up.
The four options most Louisville students choose:

Pure question-bank drill. Proven fast-path for students who want to memorize and pass. Less educational in the "understanding the why" sense, but extremely efficient. About $80 for a lifetime license. Good for students who already have aviation instincts.

Video-driven. John and Martha King explain every subject area on camera, then quiz you. More time-intensive, more genuinely educational. About $279 at list, often discounted. Good for students starting from zero.
Video + quizzes, similar to King. About $299. Well-produced, integrates with their broader course materials.
Sporty's Pilot Shop Learn to Fly course.
Traditional workbook-plus-software. Cheapest overall at $60–$90. Less polished but thorough.

There is no perfect choice. Sheppard Air gets the test passed fastest. King and Sporty's teach you more about flying while also passing the test. Gleim is the budget option. I've seen students succeed with all four.
3. Live ground instruction for the hard parts
Certain subjects are hard to self-teach:
Weather chart interpretation (METARs and TAFs are easy; prognostic charts and area forecasts take practice)
If you're hitting a wall on any of these, an hour of ground with a real instructor is usually faster than six hours of staring at a video. This is where a good ground instructor earns their fee.
This plan assumes a working adult who can commit 1–1.5 hours per weekday and a few hours on weekends.
Read the first third of the

(Chapters 1–6: aircraft structure, principles of flight, aerodynamics, flight controls, flight instruments, flight manuals). Take 10–15 practice questions per day on introductory subjects. Goal: comfortable with aircraft basics and flight instruments.

: aircraft systems, flight manuals, weight and balance, aircraft performance, weather theory. Work through weight and balance problems in your test-prep software until you get 8/10 right consistently. Practice density altitude problems. Goal: can compute a W&B and a takeoff-distance chart without help.

: weather services, airport operations, airspace, navigation. Study sectional chart symbology — the Chart Users' Guide (free PDF) is the reference. Heavy drill on airspace questions. Airspace is the single subject most students get wrong; commit to doing 30 airspace questions over the week. Goal: can identify every symbol on a sectional and classify every airspace category from memory.
Week 4: Regulations, procedures, and final review
(general operating rules). These are required reading — the test leans heavily on both. Read the

sections on flight operations, communications, and emergency procedures. Take full-length practice tests every other day. Score 85%+ consistently before scheduling the real test. Review every question you miss and trace it to the underlying FAR or handbook section.
When you hit 85%+ twice in a row cold, schedule the real test within the next 7 days. Knowledge decays. Don't let momentum go cold.
The one-week cram plan (if you already know aviation)
For students with prior aviation knowledge — a rated pilot getting back in currency, or someone who has been around aviation for years:
Full-length diagnostic test. Note weak subjects.
Drill weak subjects only. Aim for 30 questions per day in each weak area.
Second full-length test. If 85%+, you're ready.
Light review only. Don't learn new material.
This works for experienced aviation people. It does not work for someone learning the subject matter for the first time. No shortcuts on a foundation you don't have.
After watching hundreds of students work through this test, the pattern is consistent:
Boundaries, altitudes, equipment requirements, cloud clearance, visibility minimums. The airspace table is a memorization exercise and most students under-study it.
Conceptually simple, but students rush the math. Slow down and draw the envelope. Every time.
METARs and TAFs are standard-format and learnable. Area forecasts and prognostic charts are where students check out — don't.
Blue vs. magenta airport symbols. What UNICOM vs. CTAF frequencies mean. Obstacle heights. Terrain relief.
Currency requirements, recent-flight experience, medical validity periods. Memorize these; there are only about 12 of them and they come up repeatedly.
Spending extra hours on these five areas pays off more than re-reading familiar material.
psiexams.com — search "FAA Private Pilot" and pick your date.
Government-issued photo ID, your endorsement (digital or paper).
your phone into the testing room. There's a locker.
You'll want time to settle, use the restroom, and not be stressed.
You can write on scratch paper during the test.
2.5 hours for 60 questions is ~2.5 minutes per question. You have plenty of time. Don't rush.
If you score below 70, you can retake after 30 days without additional training, or sooner with additional instruction and a new endorsement.
The knowledge test result is valid for

. You have two years to complete your practical (flight) checkride. The result logs electronically with the FAA. Your test report — the printout you receive — lists which Areas of Operation you missed. Your CFI will review those with you before the practical test. Don't lose the printout.
What score do I need to pass the FAA Private Pilot written test?
Can I retake it if I fail?

Yes. FAA rules allow retakes, but you need a new endorsement — either from additional instruction or from your self-study course certification. Most students don't need to retake. The four-week plan above passes on the first try.
How long is my passing score good for?
24 calendar months from the date you pass.
Do I need to take the written before I can solo?
No. You need the written before you take the practical (checkride). Many students take the written about 70% of the way through their flight training, though earlier is smarter.

It's not cheating. You're studying from the actual question bank that the FAA publishes — the bank is public knowledge. What Sheppard does is prioritize efficient memorization of that bank. Whether that makes you a better pilot is a separate question — it doesn't, but flight training is where you become a better pilot. The written test just certifies that you've absorbed a specific body of knowledge.
How much does the whole written-test process cost?
Test fee ~$175. Software $60–$300 depending on choice. Endorsement is included if you self-study; otherwise ~$50–$100 from a ground instructor. Total: roughly $300–$500.

Take 10–15 practice questions per day on introductory subjects. Goal: comfortable with aircraft basics and flight instruments.

Read PHAK Chapters 7–11: aircraft systems, flight manuals, weight and balance, aircraft performance, weather theory. Work through weight and balance problems in your test-prep software until you get 8/10 right consistently. Practice density altitude problems. Goal: can compute a W&B and a takeoff-distance chart without help.

Read PHAK Chapters 12–15: weather services, airport operations, airspace, navigation. Study sectional chart symbology — the Chart Users' Guide (free PDF) is the reference. Heavy drill on airspace questions. Airspace is the single subject most students get wrong; commit to doing 30 airspace questions over the week. Goal: can identify every symbol on a sectional and classify every airspace category from memory.
Week 4: Regulations, procedures, and final review

Read FAR Part 61 (certification) and FAR Part 91 (general operating rules). These are required reading — the test leans heavily on both. Read the AIM sections on flight operations, communications, and emergency procedures. Take full-length practice tests every other day. Score 85%+ consistently before scheduling the real test. Review every question you miss and trace it to the underlying FAR or handbook section.
When you hit 85%+ twice in a row cold, schedule the real test within the next 7 days. Knowledge decays. Don't let momentum go cold.
The one-week cram plan (if you already know aviation)
For students with prior aviation knowledge — a rated pilot getting back in currency, or someone who has been around aviation for years:
Day 1: Full-length diagnostic test. Note weak subjects.
Days 2–4: Drill weak subjects only. Aim for 30 questions per day in each weak area.
Day 5: Second full-length test. If 85%+, you're ready.
Day 6: Light review only. Don't learn new material.
This works for experienced aviation people. It does not work for someone learning the subject matter for the first time. No shortcuts on a foundation you don't have.
After watching hundreds of students work through this test, the pattern is consistent:
Airspace. Boundaries, altitudes, equipment requirements, cloud clearance, visibility minimums. The airspace table is a memorization exercise and most students under-study it.
Weight and balance. Conceptually simple, but students rush the math. Slow down and draw the envelope. Every time.
Weather charts and reports. METARs and TAFs are standard-format and learnable. Area forecasts and prognostic charts are where students check out — don't.
Sectional chart details. Blue vs. magenta airport symbols. What UNICOM vs. CTAF frequencies mean. Obstacle heights. Terrain relief.
Regulations specifics. Currency requirements, recent-flight experience, medical validity periods. Memorize these; there are only about 12 of them and they come up repeatedly.
Spending extra hours on these five areas pays off more than re-reading familiar material.
Schedule through PSI: psiexams.com — search "FAA Private Pilot" and pick your date.
Bring: Government-issued photo ID, your endorsement (digital or paper).
Don't bring: your phone into the testing room. There's a locker.
Arrive 30 minutes early. You'll want time to settle, use the restroom, and not be stressed.
Dress comfortably. Testing rooms are typically over-air-conditioned.
You can write on scratch paper during the test. Use it.
Pacing: 2.5 hours for 60 questions is ~2.5 minutes per question. You have plenty of time. Don't rush.
If you score below 70, you can retake after 30 days without additional training, or sooner with additional instruction and a new endorsement.

The knowledge test result is valid for 24 calendar months. You have two years to complete your practical (flight) checkride. The result logs electronically with the FAA. Your test report — the printout you receive — lists which Areas of Operation you missed. Your CFI will review those with you before the practical test. Don't lose the printout.

text: Where to Take the FAA Written Test Near Louisville (PSI Testing Centers) | Diego Suarez
Where to Take the FAA Written Test Near Louisville

One of the most common points of confusion for new student pilots around Louisville: the FAA written test — officially the airman knowledge test — is not given at the airport, not given by your flight school, and not given by the FAA itself. It's given at a commercial computer testing center, on an appointment you book yourself, after an instructor signs you off. Here's the whole process, start to finish, the way I walk my ground students through it.
Who actually gives the test: PSI
FAA airman knowledge tests are administered by

, the FAA's contracted testing vendor (the centers are also still called CATS centers — Computer Assisted Testing Service — from an earlier branding). PSI runs a nationwide network of testing centers, and there are locations serving the Louisville area.

Two practical notes. First, testing center locations and hours change, so don't plan around a specific address you found in an old forum post — use PSI's test-center search when you schedule and treat the scheduler as the controlling source. Second, you schedule and pay through PSI's website (
), not by calling the center. The center is just a room full of computers; PSI's system is the front door.
Step 1: Get your FAA Tracking Number (FTN)
Before you can schedule anything, you need an FAA Tracking Number. You get it by creating an account in
(iacra.faa.gov), the FAA's airman certification system. It takes about ten minutes and costs nothing.

One warning I give every student: enter your legal name exactly as it appears on the government ID you'll bring to the test. If your IACRA profile says "Mike" and your driver's license says "Michael," you can be turned away on test day with no refund. The name has to match across IACRA, PSI, your endorsement, and your ID.

For the Private Pilot knowledge test (and most others), 14 CFR 61.35 requires an endorsement from an authorized instructor certifying that you've received ground training and are prepared for the test. The testing center will ask to see it. No endorsement, no test.
Here's the part people don't realize: the endorsement doesn't have to come from your flight instructor. An

can sign off the knowledge-test endorsement — that's me, among other people. If you're self-studying and haven't started flying yet, you can knock out the written test before you ever touch an airplane. That's often the smartest order of operations: the written is out of the way, your knowledge test results are valid for 24 calendar months, and everything you study makes your early flight lessons cheaper because you're not paying airplane rates to learn ground material.

If you finish a formal home-study course, a graduation certificate from that course can also serve as the authorization for some tests — but an instructor endorsement is the most common path, and it comes with an actual human telling you whether you're ready. If you want to know exactly what the endorsement says, my
covers the knowledge-test endorsement in plain English, and

With an FTN and an endorsement in hand, you schedule at faa.psiexams.com: create the PSI account, search for the FAA test you need (double-check the test code — PAR for Private Pilot Airplane), pick a center and a time, and pay online.
The fee for most FAA knowledge tests has been running around

. Fees change, so confirm the current amount on psiexams.com when you book. If you fail, you pay again for the retake — one more reason not to schedule until your practice-test scores say you're ready.
Schedule with margin. Testing center calendars fill up near holidays and school breaks, and if your checkride timeline depends on this test, don't book the last possible week.
What to bring on test day
— a driver's license or passport, unexpired, with the name that matches your IACRA and PSI records.
— the physical logbook endorsement or a signed graduation certificate, as applicable.

— for pilot tests you can generally bring an E6B flight computer (manual or a non-programmable electronic one), a plotter, and a basic non-programmable calculator. The center provides scratch paper and a supplement book with the figures the questions reference.
What you cannot bring into the room: your phone, smartwatch, notes, books, bags, and food. Lockers are usually provided. Leave the phone in the car if you're the type to forget.
What the testing room is actually like

If you've taken a test at a Pearson or Prometric-style center, it's the same world. You check in, show your ID and endorsement, get scanned or wanded, stash your belongings, and sit at a carrel with a computer and a camera pointed at you. The proctor can't answer questions about content — only about the computer.

The Private Pilot test is 60 multiple-choice questions with a 2.5-hour limit; 70% is passing. Most prepared students finish in well under two hours. You can flag questions and come back to them, which you should do instead of agonizing — the question you stare at for ten minutes is usually clearer after you've answered the forty easy ones.
After the test: the report matters more than the score
You get your result immediately. Whether you pass with a 72 or a 98, the testing center hands you an Airman Knowledge Test Report stamped with

for every question you missed. Keep that document — you need the original for your checkride, and those codes are a to-do list. Your instructor is required to review the deficient areas with you before the practical test, and the examiner can (and does) probe them.

If you fail: it's not the end of anything. You'll need additional training and a new endorsement before retesting, and you pay the fee again. Annoying, expensive, survivable. Better to avoid it by not scheduling until your practice tests are consistently in the 80s — my
lays out the study method I use with students.
Create an IACRA account, get your FTN, use your exact legal name.
Study until your practice scores are consistently in the mid-80s or better.
Get a knowledge-test endorsement from a CFI or AGI.
Schedule and pay at faa.psiexams.com — verify the test code and current fee.
Show up early with ID, endorsement, and an E6B. Leave the phone in the car.
Walk out with your test report and keep the original somewhere safe.
Where is the FAA testing center in Louisville?

FAA knowledge tests are given at PSI testing centers, and PSI operates locations serving the Louisville area. Addresses and hours change, so use the test-center search at faa.psiexams.com when you schedule — it's the controlling source, not an address from an old forum post.
How much does the FAA written test cost?
Most FAA airman knowledge tests have been running around $175. Fees change, so confirm the current amount at psiexams.com when you schedule. A retake costs the full fee again.
Do I need an endorsement to take the written test?

Yes for the Private Pilot test and most others — 14 CFR 61.35 requires an authorized instructor's endorsement certifying you're prepared. A flight instructor (CFI) or an Advanced Ground Instructor (AGI) can provide it, and a formal home-study course graduation certificate can also serve as authorization for some tests.
Can I take the written test before I start flying?

Yes, and it's often the smart order. An AGI can sign your endorsement without you being enrolled in flight training, and the knowledge test report is valid for 24 calendar months. Many students finish the written first so ground knowledge doesn't eat into expensive airplane time.

You'll need additional training on the deficient areas and a new endorsement before retesting (14 CFR 61.49), plus the test fee again. The test report's ACS codes tell you exactly which subject areas to fix.

text: Flying at Bowman Field (KLOU) — A Local Pilot's Guide | Diego Suarez
Flying at Bowman Field (KLOU): A Local Pilot's Guide to Louisville's Historic Airport

This guide is current as of April 22, 2026, using the FAA Chart Supplement Southeast effective March 19 – May 14, 2026, the current FAA airport diagram, and current FAA visual charts. It is educational, not a navigation source. Always check current charts, NOTAMs, ATIS, and ATC instructions before flying.

Bowman Field — KLOU on the chart — is Louisville's historic general aviation airport. It sits close to downtown, underneath and alongside Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport's Class C structure, and it has enough training, transient, business, and special-event traffic that a little preparation makes the first visit much easier.
The Louisville Regional Airport Authority traces Bowman Field's opening to

. Bowman served as Louisville's main airport before scheduled airline activity moved to what is now Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport (KSDF). Today, it remains a busy public-use general aviation field with flight training, local operators, maintenance, fuel, hangars, and a strong local pilot community.

That history is part of the experience. The field still has a classic airport feel: compact ramps, older hangars, a recognizable terminal area, and a mix of student pilots, owners, transient aircraft, and occasional special operations sharing a relatively small surface area.
Bowman Field's published field elevation is
. The airport has two paved asphalt runways:

Both runways have published displaced-threshold and declared-distance information. Use the Chart Supplement, airport diagram, and current performance planning for the runway actually assigned — don't reduce runway planning to the simple physical length.

Runway 06/24 is the longer runway and commonly handles much of the traffic flow, but wind, traffic, runway work, and tower sequencing drive the actual runway in use. Runway 15/33 is the crosswind runway and is useful when the wind does not favor 06/24.

The Chart Supplement lists 100LL, Jet A, and oxygen availability. Confirm parking and service needs with the FBO/operator you intend to use before arriving, as tenant and transient details can change.
airport during published tower hours. The current Chart Supplement lists Class D service and tower operation as
in Louisville during the current daylight-time period. Outside those hours, the airport operates as

For arrivals, listen to ATIS before calling tower. On first contact, give your position, altitude, and intentions, then let Bowman Tower assign the runway, entry, and sequencing. A first call might sound like: "Bowman Tower, Cessna One Two Three, ten northeast, three thousand five hundred, landing with Alpha."

For departures, get ATIS before engine start or taxi, contact Ground for taxi instructions, then contact Tower when ready for takeoff. If you are staying in the pattern, say so. If you are departing the area and need Louisville Approach for Class C service, flight following, or an IFR pickup, make that request early enough for tower to coordinate or advise.

Bowman has intersecting runways and close taxi/runway geometry. The airport diagram identifies hot spots near the runway intersection and Runway 06 at Taxiway A1. Read back all runway hold-short instructions and be deliberate about runway-crossing clearances.
The big local gotcha: Louisville Class C
. That is the airspace to brief around Bowman.
Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport (SDF) as Class C
Near KLOU, the SDF Class C shelf is charted
above and around the Bowman area. Bowman also has its own Class D surface area while the tower is operating.
2,200 feet MSL up to 4,500 feet MSL
Do not assume you can climb on course from KLOU without thinking about the SDF Class C shelf.
If your departure, arrival, or practice-area route will enter the Class C, establish the required two-way communication with the appropriate ATC facility.
If you are staying below the shelf, be precise with altitude discipline; KLOU's pattern and the surrounding shelves leave less vertical room than a new pilot may expect.
If tower or Louisville Approach gives you an altitude, heading, or routing, that instruction controls.
Departure procedures vary with runway, traffic, weather, and your destination. The reliable procedure is:
Tell Tower whether you are staying in the pattern, departing VFR, or departing IFR.
Follow assigned runway, heading, altitude, and frequency-change instructions.
Coordinate with Louisville Approach when you need Class C service, flight following, or an IFR clearance after departure.
The FAA publishes a special Bowman Field terminal-area graphic notice for the
This is not a casual sightseeing route — it is a named VFR departure procedure pilots should specifically request when appropriate, especially in the IFR pickup context described by the notice.
In plain language, the procedure has pilots request it by name, remain VFR at or below
initially, and use the heading and climb instructions coordinated by LOU ATC and Louisville Departure. The published weather minimums for the procedure are a
. Use the current FAA notice before flying it — don't rely on secondhand descriptions.
Bowman Tower assigns the arrival flow. For a normal VFR arrival, call with enough distance for tower to build you into traffic, then comply with the runway, pattern entry, and sequencing you receive.
For pattern altitude, the current Chart Supplement does not publish a nonstandard KLOU traffic pattern altitude. FAA standard traffic pattern altitude for propeller aircraft is
unless otherwise established. At Bowman's 546-foot field elevation, that works out to about
. If Bowman Tower assigns a different altitude or your aircraft category requires something else, follow that instruction.

Pattern discipline matters at KLOU because the field combines student pilots, faster singles, transient aircraft, and Class C coordination nearby. Keep radio calls concise, read back runway instructions clearly, and avoid adding extra chatter when the frequency is busy.

The Kentucky Derby changes Louisville flying. The FAA publishes special air traffic procedures for the Derby period, and those procedures are not optional reading if you plan to fly around Louisville that week.
, the FAA Kentucky Derby special procedures apply

for Louisville Muhammad Ali International (SDF), Bowman Field (LOU), and Clark Regional (JVY). The notice says Class C service is mandatory for VFR arrivals during the event procedures and highlights heavy traffic demand, helicopters, banner tow, and blimp operations near Churchill Downs.
For Bowman departures during the 2026 Derby procedures, the FAA notice says departing aircraft should contact
, advise IFR or VFR, and that VFR departures should not expect flight following or an IFR clearance within

Check the FAA Domestic Notice, NOTAMs, TFRs, ATIS, and any local operator guidance before every Derby-week flight. Thunder Over Louisville and VIP movements can also create temporary restrictions or unusual traffic flows.

Bowman sits in the Ohio River Valley, so local weather can change a training day quickly. Summer convection, winter low ceilings, fog or low stratus, and frontal wind shifts are all normal planning concerns. Morning and evening flights are often smoother than hot afternoons, but the current METAR, TAF, radar, convective outlooks, and instructor judgment matter more than broad seasonal rules.
The active runway is always a current-wind and tower-sequencing decision. Listen to ATIS before you build a mental picture of the departure.
A few local habits make Bowman easier to work with:
Be ready before calling Ground or Tower.
Keep radio calls short when the pattern is full.
Read back hold-short and runway-crossing instructions exactly.
Be disciplined about pattern altitude and spacing.
Expect a mix of training aircraft and faster traffic.
Treat restaurant, hangar, and ramp conversations as community, not procedure.
None of those habits replaces ATC instructions or current FAA publications. They just make you a better neighbor at a busy GA field.

What's the pattern altitude at KLOU?

The current Chart Supplement does not publish a nonstandard KLOU traffic pattern altitude. FAA standard traffic pattern altitude for propeller aircraft is 1,000 feet AGL — about 1,550 feet MSL at Bowman Field (546 ft elevation) — unless ATC assigns otherwise.
What airspace should I watch above Bowman?

Current FAA sources chart Louisville/SDF as Class C. Around KLOU, the nearby SDF Class C shelf is charted 45/22, meaning 2,200 to 4,500 feet MSL, with Bowman's own Class D surface area active during tower hours.
Can I fly through the Louisville Class C as a student pilot?

Class C operations require the proper equipment and two-way radio communication with ATC before entering the airspace. A solo student should only fly routes and airports authorized by their instructor and endorsed in their logbook.
What's the tower frequency for Bowman?
Bowman Tower is 119.5. The same frequency is published as CTAF when the tower is closed.
The current Chart Supplement lists tower/Class D service as 1200–0300Z‡, which is 0700–2200 local during the current daylight-time period. Confirm on current charts and NOTAMs before flying.
Can I land at KLOU in a Light-Sport Aircraft?
Yes, if the aircraft and pilot are legal for the operation and can comply with towered-airport procedures. KLOU is a public-use towered airport, not a special LSA-restricted field.

blocks: Flying at Bowman Field (KLOU): A Local Pilot's Guide to Louisville's Historic Airport

This guide is current as of April 22, 2026, using the FAA Chart Supplement Southeast effective March 19 – May 14, 2026, the current FAA airport diagram, and current FAA visual charts. It is educational, not a navigation source. Always check current charts, NOTAMs, ATIS, and ATC instructions before flying.

Bowman Field — KLOU on the chart — is Louisville's historic general aviation airport. It sits close to downtown, underneath and alongside Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport's Class C structure, and it has enough training, transient, business, and special-event traffic that a little preparation makes the first visit much easier.

The Louisville Regional Airport Authority traces Bowman Field's opening to 1921. Bowman served as Louisville's main airport before scheduled airline activity moved to what is now Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport (KSDF). Today, it remains a busy public-use general aviation field with flight training, local operators, maintenance, fuel, hangars, and a strong local pilot community.

That history is part of the experience. The field still has a classic airport feel: compact ramps, older hangars, a recognizable terminal area, and a mix of student pilots, owners, transient aircraft, and occasional special operations sharing a relatively small surface area.
Bowman Field's published field elevation is 546 feet MSL. The airport has two paved asphalt runways:

Both runways have published displaced-threshold and declared-distance information. Use the Chart Supplement, airport diagram, and current performance planning for the runway actually assigned — don't reduce runway planning to the simple physical length.

Runway 06/24 is the longer runway and commonly handles much of the traffic flow, but wind, traffic, runway work, and tower sequencing drive the actual runway in use. Runway 15/33 is the crosswind runway and is useful when the wind does not favor 06/24.

The Chart Supplement lists 100LL, Jet A, and oxygen availability. Confirm parking and service needs with the FBO/operator you intend to use before arriving, as tenant and transient details can change.

Bowman is a towered Class D airport during published tower hours. The current Chart Supplement lists Class D service and tower operation as 1200–0300Z‡, which corresponds to 0700–2200 local time in Louisville during the current daylight-time period. Outside those hours, the airport operates as Class E.

For arrivals, listen to ATIS before calling tower. On first contact, give your position, altitude, and intentions, then let Bowman Tower assign the runway, entry, and sequencing. A first call might sound like: "Bowman Tower, Cessna One Two Three, ten northeast, three thousand five hundred, landing with Alpha."

For departures, get ATIS before engine start or taxi, contact Ground for taxi instructions, then contact Tower when ready for takeoff. If you are staying in the pattern, say so. If you are departing the area and need Louisville Approach for Class C service, flight following, or an IFR pickup, make that request early enough for tower to coordinate or advise.

Bowman has intersecting runways and close taxi/runway geometry. The airport diagram identifies hot spots near the runway intersection and Runway 06 at Taxiway A1. Read back all runway hold-short instructions and be deliberate about runway-crossing clearances.
The big local gotcha: Louisville Class C
Current FAA sources chart Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport (SDF) as Class C. That is the airspace to brief around Bowman.

Near KLOU, the SDF Class C shelf is charted 45/22, meaning the shelf extends from 2,200 feet MSL up to 4,500 feet MSL above and around the Bowman area. Bowman also has its own Class D surface area while the tower is operating.
Do not assume you can climb on course from KLOU without thinking about the SDF Class C shelf.
If your departure, arrival, or practice-area route will enter the Class C, establish the required two-way communication with the appropriate ATC facility.
If you are staying below the shelf, be precise with altitude discipline; KLOU's pattern and the surrounding shelves leave less vertical room than a new pilot may expect.
If tower or Louisville Approach gives you an altitude, heading, or routing, that instruction controls.
Departure procedures vary with runway, traffic, weather, and your destination. The reliable procedure is:
Tell Tower whether you are staying in the pattern, departing VFR, or departing IFR.
Follow assigned runway, heading, altitude, and frequency-change instructions.
Coordinate with Louisville Approach when you need Class C service, flight following, or an IFR clearance after departure.

The FAA publishes a special Bowman Field terminal-area graphic notice for the "Air Devil Departure." This is not a casual sightseeing route — it is a named VFR departure procedure pilots should specifically request when appropriate, especially in the IFR pickup context described by the notice.

In plain language, the procedure has pilots request it by name, remain VFR at or below 2,500 feet initially, and use the heading and climb instructions coordinated by LOU ATC and Louisville Departure. The published weather minimums for the procedure are a 3,000-foot ceiling and 3 miles visibility. Use the current FAA notice before flying it — don't rely on secondhand descriptions.
Bowman Tower assigns the arrival flow. For a normal VFR arrival, call with enough distance for tower to build you into traffic, then comply with the runway, pattern entry, and sequencing you receive.

For pattern altitude, the current Chart Supplement does not publish a nonstandard KLOU traffic pattern altitude. FAA standard traffic pattern altitude for propeller aircraft is 1,000 feet AGL unless otherwise established. At Bowman's 546-foot field elevation, that works out to about 1,550 feet MSL. If Bowman Tower assigns a different altitude or your aircraft category requires something else, follow that instruction.

Pattern discipline matters at KLOU because the field combines student pilots, faster singles, transient aircraft, and Class C coordination nearby. Keep radio calls concise, read back runway instructions clearly, and avoid adding extra chatter when the frequency is busy.

The Kentucky Derby changes Louisville flying. The FAA publishes special air traffic procedures for the Derby period, and those procedures are not optional reading if you plan to fly around Louisville that week.

For 2026, the FAA Kentucky Derby special procedures apply April 29 – May 3, 2026 for Louisville Muhammad Ali International (SDF), Bowman Field (LOU), and Clark Regional (JVY). The notice says Class C service is mandatory for VFR arrivals during the event procedures and highlights heavy traffic demand, helicopters, banner tow, and blimp operations near Churchill Downs.

For Bowman departures during the 2026 Derby procedures, the FAA notice says departing aircraft should contact Clearance Delivery on 118.90 and Ground on 121.80, advise IFR or VFR, and that VFR departures should not expect flight following or an IFR clearance within 50 miles of SDF.

Check the FAA Domestic Notice, NOTAMs, TFRs, ATIS, and any local operator guidance before every Derby-week flight. Thunder Over Louisville and VIP movements can also create temporary restrictions or unusual traffic flows.

Bowman sits in the Ohio River Valley, so local weather can change a training day quickly. Summer convection, winter low ceilings, fog or low stratus, and frontal wind shifts are all normal planning concerns. Morning and evening flights are often smoother than hot afternoons, but the current METAR, TAF, radar, convective outlooks, and instructor judgment matter more than broad seasonal rules.
The active runway is always a current-wind and tower-sequencing decision. Listen to ATIS before you build a mental picture of the departure.
A few local habits make Bowman easier to work with:
Be ready before calling Ground or Tower.
Keep radio calls short when the pattern is full.
Read back hold-short and runway-crossing instructions exactly.
Be disciplined about pattern altitude and spacing.
Expect a mix of training aircraft and faster traffic.
Treat restaurant, hangar, and ramp conversations as community, not procedure.
None of those habits replaces ATC instructions or current FAA publications. They just make you a better neighbor at a busy GA field.

text: How to Choose a Flight School in Louisville Without Regret | Diego Suarez
How to Choose a Flight School in Louisville Without Regret

Nobody in Louisville writes this article, and I understand why — every flight school that publishes "how to choose a flight school" is really publishing "choose us." I'm a flight instructor and ground instructor at Bowman Field (KLOU), not a flight school, so I can afford to be more honest than a brochure. What follows is the framework I walk people through when they ask me where they should learn to fly. It applies whether you end up training at Bowman Field, at Clark Regional (KJVY) across the river in Jeffersonville, with an independent CFI, or anywhere else.
The short version: you're not choosing a school, you're choosing an instructor and a cadence. Everything else is secondary.
Start with the outcome you actually want
"I want to learn to fly" covers at least four different goals, and each one points at a different kind of provider:
A Sport or Private certificate through a local Part 61 operation or an independent CFI is usually the right shape. You don't need an academy.
"I want to fly for fun, locally, a few times a month."
Private certificate, and think ahead about the aircraft you'll actually rent afterward — a four-seat 172 matters more to you than a two-seat sport airplane.

Now a structured Part 141 program or a fast-track academy enters the conversation, because total time and recruiting pipelines start to matter. That's a different budget and a different lifestyle commitment.
"I want to fly for the airlines."
Then your first decision isn't a school at all — it's a discovery flight. More on that below.

Be suspicious of any provider that gives you the same pitch regardless of which of those you are. A school that tries to sell a career-track program to someone who wants to fly over the Ohio River on Saturdays is telling you what they optimize for.
Part 61 vs. Part 141, in plain English
These are the two FAA rule sets a school can operate under. The difference that actually matters to a student:

schools run an FAA-approved syllabus with stage checks and a defined structure. The legal minimum hours are lower, the schedule is more rigid, and the environment feels more like a school. Good fit for full-time students and career tracks.

is the flexible path — most local schools and every independent CFI operate here. Training follows your pace and your schedule. The realistic total hours are usually similar regardless of what the minimums say; FAA public guidance puts the national average around 60–75 hours for a Private certificate.

Neither is inherently better. A motivated twice-a-week Part 61 student will finish faster and cheaper than a disengaged Part 141 student. Structure helps people who need structure. Flexibility helps people who have jobs.
The instructor matters more than the school

You will spend 50-plus hours in a small airplane with one person. The school's paint job, website, and fleet count for almost nothing compared to whether that person teaches well and fits how you learn.

What good instructor fit looks like: they explain things in a way that clicks for you, they debrief every flight with specifics instead of "good job," they show up prepared, and they tell you what you did wrong without making you feel stupid. What bad fit looks like: you dread lessons, you can't predict what mood you're getting, or you realize you're re-learning the same maneuver for the fourth lesson with no diagnosis of why it isn't sticking.

Ask any school who you'd actually fly with, and ask to meet that person before you commit money. If the answer is "whoever is on the schedule," understand that you're buying a lottery ticket. Instructor turnover is real in this industry — instructors build time and leave for the airlines — so also ask what happens when your instructor moves on.
You don't need to be an aircraft expert to read a fleet. Three questions cover most of it:
A school with three airplanes and one perpetually in maintenance has a scheduling problem you'll feel within a month. At a small field like Bowman, you can literally stand on the ramp and count.
How many trainers do they actually have, and how many are flying?
A row of identical, well-used trainers is a good sign. One gleaming flagship surrounded by tired airframes tells you where the money goes.
Is the fleet for training or for show?

If you're going Sport Pilot, they need a legal LSA on the line. If you want to train in a 172 because that's what you'll rent later, fly a 172. If you're curious about the tradeoffs between the two most common training types at Bowman, I wrote a
Does the aircraft match your goal?
Hourly rate is not total cost

Every school advertises an hourly airplane rate. Almost none advertise what you'll actually spend, because the real number is (hourly rate) × (hours you need), and the hours are the bigger variable. A school that's $15/hour cheaper on the airplane but schedules you once every two weeks will cost you thousands more in re-learning than the school that flies you twice a week.

When you compare, compare wet rate to wet rate (fuel included), get the instructor rate separately, and ask what a realistic total looks like for a student like you — then compare that to the honest Louisville numbers in my
. If a school's implied total is dramatically below that range, they're quoting you the FAA minimum, not your likely finish.

This is the unglamorous factor that decides whether you finish. Ask directly: if I want to fly twice a week, can this operation actually deliver that? Twice-a-week means two aircraft slots and two instructor slots, every week, through Derby week, through August maintenance, through the instructor's vacation.

Ask how far out the schedule is booked right now. Ask what their cancellation policy is and what happens when weather cancels — do you roll to the next open slot, or the next open slot after everyone else's standing bookings? The
is brutal on this point: a student flying twice a week finishes in months; the same student flying twice a month can take years and spend more getting there.
You can learn a lot from how a school treats inconvenient safety questions:
Ask what happens when a pilot reports a squawk on an airplane. Good answer: it's grounded until maintenance signs it off. Bad answer: a long pause.
Ask how they handle weather minimums for students. Good schools have written student solo limits stricter than the legal ones.
Ask whether they do stage checks or progress checks with a second instructor. A school that checks its own instructors' work is a school that takes training seriously.
Watch the ramp. Are preflights happening, or are people hopping in and going? Do the instructors walk around the airplane every time?
Questions to ask on the introductory visit
Bring this list. A school that answers these well has nothing to hide:
Who would I actually train with, and can I meet them?
What are your aircraft and instructor rates, wet, in writing?
What do your Private Pilot students actually average in total hours — not the FAA minimum?
If I want to fly twice a week, when could we start, and how often does that schedule actually hold?
What happens to my money if I pay ahead and quit? (Get the refund policy in writing.)
What happens when my instructor leaves or goes to the airlines?
How is maintenance handled, and who decides an airplane is grounded?
What are your student solo weather minimums?
Can I talk to a current student and a recent graduate?
Do you require a deposit or block payment, and why?
Red flags worth walking away from
Pay-as-you-go is standard at independent instructors and most Part 61 operations in Louisville. Big upfront money transfers all the risk to you.
Large non-refundable deposits or pressure to prepay a big block.
Almost nobody finishes at minimums. It's not a lie, exactly — it's a number chosen because it's small.
Quoting the FAA 40-hour minimum as your expected finish.
You can't meet your instructor before paying.
A school that sells by tearing down the other options at Bowman or across the river at KJVY is telling you they can't sell on their own merits.
"Sure, any time you want" from a school with two airplanes is a scheduling promise that will break.
The discovery flight is the test drive
Before you commit to anything, fly. A

is an hour in the left seat with an instructor, and it's the single best data-gathering tool you have. You learn whether you love flying, and — just as valuable — you learn how this operation treats a new customer. Did they brief you? Did they answer questions honestly, including "is this a smart use of my money"? Did it feel like instruction or like a sales pitch?
Do a discovery flight at more than one place if you're torn. It's the cheapest comparison shopping in aviation.
What you lose by picking wrong — and how to leave

The cost of a bad fit isn't just money. It's the three months you spend not progressing, and the very real chance you quit flying entirely believing you weren't cut out for it. I've talked to students who thought they were slow learners; they were just badly taught.

If you're mid-training and it's not working: you're allowed to leave. Get your logbook (it's yours), get any prepaid balance refund per the written policy, and take your records to the next instructor. A good CFI will pick up your training where it stands, verify what's solid, and move on. No loyalty is owed to a situation that isn't working.

In the interest of the honesty this article runs on: I'm not a flight school. I'm an FAA Certificated Flight Instructor and Advanced Ground Instructor based at Bowman Field. I do ground instruction, written-test prep, endorsement sign-offs within my ratings, discovery flights, and training-path planning, within my ratings, aircraft access, and availability. For plenty of students, the right answer is a school with a fleet and full-time staff, and I'll say so in the first conversation if that's you. For others — especially people who want ground-first, cost-controlled training with a plan before they start burning airplane hours — working with an independent instructor is the better shape. Either way, the framework above applies.
How many flight schools are there in the Louisville area?

A handful of training providers operate out of Bowman Field (KLOU) in Louisville, plus options at Clark Regional (KJVY) in Jeffersonville and independent CFIs who teach in rented or customer aircraft. The exact lineup changes, so verify who's currently operating before building a shortlist.
Is a Part 141 school better than Part 61 for a hobby pilot?

Usually not. Part 141 structure is built for full-time and career-track students. A recreational student flying around a work schedule is typically better served by the flexibility of Part 61 — either a local Part 61 school or an independent instructor.
Should I pay for a big block of flight time up front?

Be cautious. Pay-as-you-go is standard in the Louisville Part 61 market and keeps the risk on the provider's side. If a school wants a large non-refundable prepayment, get the refund policy in writing and ask yourself why they need your money that badly.
Can I switch instructors or schools mid-training?

Yes. Your logbook and training records are yours. A new instructor will review what's been done, verify it's solid, and continue from there. Switching costs some momentum, but staying in a bad fit costs more.
What's the single best way to evaluate a school?
Book a discovery flight. One hour in the left seat tells you more about the operation, the instructor, and whether flying is for you than any website or tour. Do it before you commit money anywhere.

text: Flying During Kentucky Derby Week: TFRs and What KLOU Pilots Need to Know | Diego Suarez
Flying During Kentucky Derby Week: TFRs and What KLOU Pilots Need to Know

Every spring, the biggest horse race on earth happens about four miles from the departure end of Bowman Field's runways. The Kentucky Derby is great for Louisville and genuinely complicated for Louisville aviation: temporary flight restrictions over Churchill Downs, special FAA procedures at three local airports, a flood of charter and private traffic into KSDF, helicopters and banner tows in the pattern's neighborhood, and — if a VIP attends — restrictions on top of restrictions.
If you fly or train out of Bowman Field (KLOU), here's how Derby week actually works from the cockpit side. One rule frames everything below:
Dates, TFR dimensions, altitudes, and procedures are republished annually. This article teaches you what to expect and where to check — it does not replace the current NOTAM.

Around Derby — typically for the big race days at the end of the meet, and often for the Kentucky Oaks the day before — the FAA establishes a temporary flight restriction over Churchill Downs. In recent years it has been in the neighborhood of a few nautical miles around the track, from the surface up to a few thousand feet, active for a block of hours around the races.

Don't plan around those numbers. Plan around the process: the exact radius, ceiling, and active times are published in a NOTAM each year, and the NOTAM is the only version that counts. Churchill Downs sits close enough to Bowman Field that a TFR of even modest size changes what a normal training flight looks like — some pattern work and practice-area routes that are routine in March are simply not available during the active window.

What happens if you bust a TFR? At best, a very uncomfortable conversation with the FAA. At worst, certificate action — and during a nationally televised security event, intercept procedures are not theoretical. This is the one airspace violation with essentially zero slack.
The FAA's Derby special procedures notice

Separate from the TFR, the FAA publishes special air traffic procedures for the Derby period each year, covering Louisville Muhammad Ali International (KSDF), Bowman Field (KLOU), and Clark Regional (KJVY). The 2026 version, for example, ran April 29 through May 3 and made Class C service mandatory for VFR arrivals during the event procedures, with explicit warnings about heavy traffic demand, helicopter operations, banner towing, and blimp operations near Churchill Downs.

That notice also changes how you depart. In the 2026 procedures, Bowman departures were directed to contact Clearance Delivery on 118.90 before Ground, and VFR departures were told not to expect flight following or an IFR clearance within 50 miles of SDF. Next year's numbers and frequencies may differ — the point is that the normal "call Ground, taxi, call Tower" rhythm gets a Derby-week overlay, and you're expected to have read it. My
keeps the current event procedures summarized as they're published.
guide to flying at Bowman Field
Thunder Over Louisville starts it all

The Derby festival's opening act, Thunder Over Louisville, is one of the largest airshows and fireworks displays in the country, held on the downtown riverfront a couple of weeks before the race. It comes with its own temporary restrictions along the Ohio River, its own surge of transient traffic, and a rehearsal day that also affects the airspace. If you're a student pilot, treat the entire festival stretch — Thunder through Derby — as a period where NOTAMs are required reading before every flight, not just on race day.
What Derby week means for training at Bowman Field
Practically, here's what I tell students to expect:
If a TFR window overlaps your scheduled pattern work, the lesson becomes a ground session or reschedules. Nobody at KLOU fights this; it's one week a year.
Some lessons will move or cancel.

Charter and transient traffic surges across the area, fuel trucks are busy, and the ramp has airplanes you don't normally see. Stay heads-up on the surface — Bowman already has intersecting runways and published hot spots.
The airport gets busy in a different way.
Helicopters, banner tows, and blimps operate at altitudes students share. See-and-avoid stops being a checkbox phrase this week.
Noise and traffic in the practice areas.
Seriously. Weather briefings, airspace study, cross-country planning, written-test prep — the smart play is banking ground progress while the airspace is complicated.
It's a great week for ground school.
Current NOTAMs, the event procedures notice, ATIS, and a conversation with your instructor or a briefer. Not your memory of last year.
Flights that do happen need real briefings.
Make this the preflight habit for late April and early May:
— through your EFB (ForeFlight/Garmin Pilot flag them graphically), the FAA's NOTAM search, or a call to Flight Service at 1-800-WX-BRIEF. Search both KLOU and KSDF.
— published annually for SDF, LOU, and JVY. Read the current year's, not an old copy.
The FAA's Derby special procedures notice
— Derby-week ATIS at Bowman carries event-specific notes.
— local guidance consolidates fast that week. Ask.

Derby week is also when Louisville is most worth flying around. On the unrestricted days between events, the city is dressed up, the riverfront is busy, and evening flights over the Ohio are about as good as local flying gets. The pilots who enjoy that week are the ones who checked the NOTAMs that morning — and the ones who watched the race from a backyard instead of a cockpit, like everyone else.
Is there really a TFR over Churchill Downs during the Kentucky Derby?

Yes. The FAA establishes temporary flight restrictions over Churchill Downs around the major race days each year. The exact radius, altitude, and active times are published in NOTAMs annually and change — check the current NOTAM rather than planning around a prior year's numbers.
Can student pilots fly out of Bowman Field during Derby week?

Often yes, but not always — it depends on the TFR windows and event procedures in effect for that specific day. Some lessons fly normally, some get rerouted, and some become ground sessions. Check NOTAMs and ATIS before every flight that week, and coordinate with your instructor.
What airports do the Derby special procedures cover?

The FAA's annual Derby procedures notice covers Louisville Muhammad Ali International (KSDF), Bowman Field (KLOU), and Clark Regional (KJVY). Procedures have included mandatory Class C service for VFR arrivals and special departure flows — read the current year's notice for the actual requirements.
Does Thunder Over Louisville affect flying too?

Yes. Thunder Over Louisville, the airshow and fireworks event on the downtown riverfront a couple of weeks before the Derby, brings its own temporary restrictions along the Ohio River, plus a rehearsal day. Treat the whole festival stretch as mandatory-NOTAM-check territory.
What happens if you accidentally fly into a TFR?

Expect anything from an FAA investigation and certificate action to, during a major security event, interception by military or law enforcement aircraft. There is effectively no slack on TFR violations — which is why checking NOTAMs before every Derby-week flight is non-negotiable.
